parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: State, for an X-ray image, what is meant by:

markscheme_points.text: ease with which edges can be distinguished

hints: Hint 1: Think about looking at the boundary between bone and soft tissue on an X-ray - what makes that boundary look crisp and clear rather than blurred?
parts.proper_answer: Sharpness is the ease with which the edges of structures can be distinguished on the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what sharp means in everyday photos**
Imagine a photograph of a person. If it is sharp, you can see exactly where their hair ends and the background begins. If it is unsharp, that edge is fuzzy and spread out. The same idea applies to an X-ray.

Step 2: **Apply to X-ray diagnosis**
A good X-ray needs clear boundaries between different tissues, for example between a fracture line and intact bone. So sharpness is all about how well edges are defined, not about how dark or light the image is.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about shades of grey on the film - what makes bone stand out as white against darker soft tissue?
parts.proper_answer: Contrast is the difference in the degrees of blackening between different parts of the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate sharpness from darkness**
Sharpness was about edges. Contrast is different - it is about light versus dark. On X-ray film, more X-rays reaching the film causes more blackening.

Step 2: **Link to different tissues**
Bone absorbs more X-rays so it appears lighter (less blackening), while soft tissue transmits more so it appears darker (more blackening). The difference in that blackening between areas is the contrast, and good contrast lets you tell tissues apart.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A parallel X-ray beam passes through a thickness of $2.3\text{ cm}$ of soft body tissue. The intensity of the emerging beam is $12\%$ of the intensity of the incident beam.

Calculate the linear attenuation (absorption) coefficient $\mu$ of the soft body tissue. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what fraction of the beam gets through - you are told the emerging intensity is 12% of the incident intensity after 2.3 cm, so think about how intensity falls off exponentially with thickness.
Hint 2: Write the attenuation law as $I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$ and substitute $I/I_0 = 0.12$ and $x = 2.3 \text{ cm}$ to form an equation for $\mu$.
Hint 3: Take natural logs of both sides to isolate $\mu$, then calculate the value and remember $\mu$ has unit of inverse length, matching the cm used for $x$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the attenuation law**
X-rays are absorbed exponentially in matter. The transmitted intensity $I$ after thickness $x$ is related to incident intensity $I_0$ by: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ where $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient. A larger $\mu$ means more strongly absorbing material.

Step 2: **Insert the transmission ratio**
Here $x = 2.3 \text{ cm}$ and: $$\frac{I}{I_0} = 12\% = 0.12$$ So: $$0.12 = \exp(-\mu \times 2.3)$$

Step 3: **Solve with natural logs**
Take $\ln$ of both sides: $$\ln(0.12) = -\mu \times 2.3$$ $$-2.12 = -2.3\mu$$ $$\mu = \frac{2.12}{2.3} = 0.92 \text{ cm}^{-1}$$ The unit is $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (or $92 \text{ m}^{-1}$) because $\mu x$ must be dimensionless.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
In medical diagnosis, X-rays may be used to produce a single X-ray image or may be used in computed tomography (CT scanning).

Suggest an advantage and a disadvantage of CT scanning compared with single X-ray imaging for diagnosis.
hints: Hint 1: Think about how a single X-ray gives only one flat shadow view, while a CT scanner rotates around the patient taking many slices - what extra information does that give?
Hint 2: Think about the cost of taking many X-ray views from different angles instead of just one - what does that mean for the patient's total radiation exposure?
parts.proper_answer: Advantage: CT scanning produces a 3-dimensional image (detailed cross-sectional slices) allowing structures at different depths to be distinguished. Disadvantage: CT involves a much greater radiation exposure / dose to the patient than a single X-ray.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why CT gives more information**
A single X-ray is a 2D projection - all structures along the beam path overlap. In CT, the X-ray tube rotates around the body and a computer reconstructs many thin slices. Stacking the slices gives a full 3-dimensional view, so a tumour behind bone is no longer hidden.

Step 2: **Why CT has a drawback**
That 3D view needs hundreds of exposures from different angles. Each exposure adds dose. So the total ionising radiation dose, with its increased risk of cell damage, is much larger for CT than for one plain X-ray. That is why CT is used only when the extra detail is needed.
